name: Chinaryan v. City of Los Angeles
court: Ninth Circuit (from the Central District of California)
citation: Nos. 21-56237 and 22-55168 (9th Cir. Aug. 14, 2024) (published opinion; Federal Reporter citation not confirmed from the source read)
topic: High risk vehicle stop at gunpoint on a mistaken stolen vehicle suspicion; proning and handcuffing a compliant driver and two passengers; Fourth Amendment detention and force; qualified immunity under Washington v. Lambert and Green v. City and County of San Francisco; Monell jury instructions; the Bane Act
summary: A mother driving her teenage daughter and a friend home was followed for ten minutes, then stopped by about a dozen LAPD officers and a helicopter, ordered out at gunpoint, made to lie prone in the street, and handcuffed with her passengers because a DMV error made her black Suburban look cold plated and a similar Suburban had been stolen nearby. The handcuffs stayed on about nine minutes after officers learned of the DMV error. The Ninth Circuit held that, on the plaintiffs' version of the facts, the officers were not entitled to qualified immunity, because Washington v. Lambert and Green had clearly established that reasonable suspicion of vehicle theft alone does not justify high risk tactics absent a case specific need, and it ordered a new trial against the officers. It affirmed the defense verdict for the City on the failure to train claim because the plaintiffs' proposed jury instructions misstated the law.
coverage: The opinion was read in full, including the staff summary, all 13 footnotes of the majority, and Judge Forrest's partial dissent, from the Ninth Circuit's opinion datastore at https://cdn.ca9.uscourts.gov/datastore/opinions/2024/08/14/21-56237.pdf. The filing date of August 14, 2024 was found by probing the datastore for the docket number across June through September 2024; the file exists only under that date.

The docket numbers 21-56237 and 22-55168, the argument date of July 21, 2023, the filing date of August 14, 2024, and the panel (S. R. Thomas, Nguyen, and Forrest, Circuit Judges; Nguyen writing; Forrest dissenting in part) were confirmed from that file. The slip opinion does not print a Federal Reporter citation, and none was confirmed from any source read; the citation field gives the docket numbers and date instead.

The district court's summary judgment order, the trial record, and the jury instructions beyond what the opinion quotes were not read. The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them, viewing disputed matters in the plaintiffs' favor as the summary judgment standard required.

Washington v. Lambert, 98 F.3d 1181 (9th Cir. 1996), and Green v. City and County of San Francisco, 751 F.3d 1039 (9th Cir. 2014), are described as this opinion describes them; they were not read for this brief. The result on remand was not researched.
facts:
The facts are as the Ninth Circuit stated them, resolving disputes in the plaintiffs' favor on review of summary judgment (slip op. at 8 n. 3).

On June 14, 2019, a black 2015 Chevrolet Suburban limousine was stolen. The next evening an LAPD helicopter detected its LoJack signal, and officers traced it to an industrial area of Glenoaks Boulevard but could not recover it that night (at 6).

On June 16, Hasmik Chinaryan was driving her teenage daughter and a friend, Mariana Manukyan, home from a Father's Day gathering in her husband's black 2018 Suburban limousine, which looked very similar to the stolen one. Sergeant Cueto saw it less than half a mile from where the signal had been detected and ran the plate, which came back to a Dodge Ram that had not been reported stolen. Suspecting a cold plated car, Cueto called for backup, including a helicopter, and followed for about ten minutes. Chinaryan did not speed, drive evasively, or break any traffic law. Her windows were tinted, but Officer Gonzalez saw two people through the front windshield as he passed. About a dozen officers joined (at 7).

Chinaryan pulled over to let the police pass as they activated sirens. Officer Meneses ordered her to turn off the car, throw out the keys, step out with hands up, walk into the right lane, lie on her stomach with arms out, and turn her head away. Several officers pointed pistols at or toward her. She lay prone about three minutes and twenty-five seconds while officers cleared the car, then was handcuffed. Gonzalez and Officer Piche ordered the daughter and Manukyan out one at a time with an AR15 rifle and a shotgun pointed in their direction, had them walk fifteen to twenty steps backward, and Officer Potter handcuffed them. The daughter cried and urinated on herself from fear (at 8-9).

Officers then checked the VIN. DMV records showed a 2018 Suburban registered to Levon Chinaryan with a plate one digit off from the plates on the car, not reported stolen. Gonzalez told Meneses, "It's not stolen. The number is one off," and opined that DMV had issued the wrong plates. After another officer checked the engine block VIN and reported "All the VINs match," Cueto had the handcuffs removed. The stop lasted 24 minutes; the three remained handcuffed about nine minutes after the DMV error became apparent (at 9-10, 21).

LAPD trains three stop types: a traffic stop; a tactical investigatory stop from cover, occupants ordered out and told to lift clothing and turn, weapons holstered; and a high risk stop with weapons drawn at low ready and the suspect proned (at 10-11). The district court granted the officers summary judgment on qualified immunity and the Bane Act. The Monell failure to train claim went to trial, and the jury found for the City and LAPD (at 11-12).
holding:
Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded for a new trial on all claims against the individual officers. Judge Nguyen wrote for the majority; Judge Forrest dissented in part.

The Fourth Amendment violation, on the plaintiffs' facts. The Fourth Amendment protects people "from the terrifying and humiliating experience of being pulled from their cars at gunpoint, handcuffed, or made to lie face down on the pavement when insufficient reason for such intrusive police conduct exists" (quoting Washington). Such tactics during a Terry stop require special circumstances and are judged by objective reasonableness under the totality of the circumstances. The intrusion here was severe: removal from the car, proning, handcuffing (which "substantially aggravates the intrusiveness" of a Terry stop), and guns aimed at or near compliant people (slip op. at 13-14). The officers had no articulable basis to think these occupants posed a threat beyond the generic threat of a suspected car thief. They were cooperative, not fleeing, not known to be armed, and the theft was two nights old and nonviolent. Any safety justification for handcuffs "weakened considerably" once the DMV error became apparent, "[y]et plaintiffs were inexplicably restrained for several additional minutes." Reasonable suspicion of theft, standing alone, was not enough (at 14-15).

Clearly established. Green addressed facts like these: a woman stopped at gunpoint, ordered to her knees, and handcuffed because a plate reader misread her plate by one digit; a jury could find the stolen vehicle suspicion alone did not make her an immediate threat. The defendants' distinctions failed. They had, if anything, less certainty than the Green officers; nightfall and tinted windows did not help, because Green occurred in the dark and a tactical investigatory stop from cover was an available, less intrusive alternative; and any tinted window justification ended when the car was cleared, yet the handcuffs stayed on about nine minutes more. Washington and Green set no bright line rules, but they "established that for summary judgment purposes, reasonable suspicion of vehicle theft alone is not enough to justify the intrusive tactics used here absent some case-specific need for them" (at 16-22). The court declined to grant the plaintiffs summary judgment; Green left the question to the jury (at 22-23).

Harmless error. The defendants forfeited any argument that the Monell verdict cured the error, and it was not harmless: the jury was told the officers followed official policy, was asked about the officers collectively, and was confined to the high risk tactics rather than each officer's full conduct, including the length of handcuffing (at 24-30).

Monell instructions. The judgment for the City and LAPD was affirmed. The proposed Washington instruction treated four special circumstances as exhaustive when Washington offered them as examples, and the proposed Green instruction stated as a rule what Green held only to be a permissible inference. Like Tennessee v. Garner as explained in Scott v. Harris, Washington applies the reasonableness test rather than creating a new rule, and the model excessive force instruction adequately covered the theory (at 30-33).

Bane Act. Specific intent may be shown by reckless disregard of a clearly delineated right and is ordinarily for the jury. Cueto's statements that a high risk stop was "a given" for a cold plated car and "I had no choice," and Gonzalez's statement that he used high risk tactics because he believed the car stolen, would let a jury infer a routine practice and a refusal to exercise discretion; the delay in uncuffing could reflect cavalier indifference (at 33-35).
dissent: Judge Forrest dissented from the reversal of summary judgment on the section 1983 and Bane Act claims. In her view the defendants had raised harmless error by pointing to the jury verdict, the plaintiffs had understood and answered the argument, and the verdict for the City resolved the only question that mattered to the officers' liability: whether the officers violated the plaintiffs' Fourth Amendment rights. The jury was instructed to consider the intrusiveness, methods, restrictions on liberty, and length of the stop, the plaintiffs argued the guns, the proning, and the roughly ten minutes of handcuffing as separate violations, and the verdict form asked whether officers "acting individually or together" deprived the plaintiffs of their rights. Because the jury answered no, she would have affirmed in full (slip op. at 35-44). She joined the holding that the district court properly refused the plaintiffs' proposed instructions.
notDecided:
Whether the officers in fact violated the Fourth Amendment. The court held that a jury could so find on the plaintiffs' version of the facts and that the law was clearly established; it rejected the plaintiffs' request for judgment in their favor and sent all claims against the officers to a new trial (slip op. at 22-23, 30). The officers disputed, among other things, whether they pointed weapons directly at the plaintiffs (at 8 n. 3).

Whether a high risk stop on a suspected stolen vehicle is ever permissible without more. The court said Green necessarily carved out an exception to Washington's broader language where officers reasonably believe a vehicle is stolen and know nothing about the occupants, and that whether the generic dangers of such a stop justify high risk tactics is an inherently factual question for a jury (at 22-23).

Whether the City's policy was unconstitutional or its training deficient. The jury found for the City, and the court affirmed on the instructions; it did not pass on the policy's constitutionality (at 30-33).

The applicable harmless error standard where a claim is wrongly kept from a jury. The court found it unnecessary to decide (at 26-27).

Whether the obviousness exception to the need for a factually similar precedent applied; the plaintiffs did not argue it (at 17 n. 7).
inPractice:
Chinaryan is taught in the handcuffing and detention line with Washington v. Lambert and Green, and its message is about matching the level of intrusion to the information actually in hand. The officers had a plate that came back to a different vehicle, a similar vehicle stolen two nights earlier nearby, a ten minute follow with no evasive driving or traffic violation, and no information that anyone in the car was armed or had committed a violent crime. On those facts, the court said, a jury could find that guns, proning, and handcuffs were too much, and that the law had said so since Green in 2014.

The court did not say high risk stops of suspected stolen cars are forbidden. It said suspicion of theft alone is not enough on summary judgment, and that the officers' own training described a less intrusive option: the tactical investigatory stop from cover, weapons holstered. That trained alternative was part of the court's reasoning. Officers should be able to explain why a particular stop called for the higher tier rather than the one below it.

The clock matters as much as the tactics. The court repeatedly returned to the roughly nine minutes the family stayed handcuffed after an officer had already said "It's not stolen" and attributed the mismatch to a DMV error. A detention must end when its purpose is served, and a theory pursued after that point has to be reasonable on its own.

Finally, the sergeant's words were evidence. "It's going to be a given" and "I had no choice" let a jury infer a routine of high risk stops for every cold plated car and a refusal to exercise discretion. Routine is not a justification; it is a liability theory.
trainIt:
Train vehicle stops as a decision between tiers, not as a default to the highest tier. LAPD's three categories, traffic stop, tactical investigatory stop from cover, and high risk stop with weapons at low ready and proning, gave the court the vocabulary for its holding. Teach officers to name the tier they are choosing and the facts that justify it: information that occupants are armed, a recent violent crime, flight or noncompliance, or other articulable special circumstances. "The car might be stolen" supplies reasonable suspicion for the stop but does not by itself justify guns, proning, and handcuffs.

Train de-escalation of the tier in real time. The court said any tinted window justification ended when the car was cleared about five minutes in, and any safety justification for handcuffs weakened considerably once the DMV error was apparent. Build scenarios in which new information arrives mid-stop and require officers to lower the tier, remove restraints, and say why, with the clock running.

Train the handcuff decision separately from the stop decision. Handcuffing substantially aggravates the intrusiveness of a Terry stop. Cuffs on a compliant person need their own reason and their own end point.

Train supervisors on the words they use at scenes. The sergeant's statements that a high risk stop was a given and that he had no choice were the evidence that kept the Bane Act claim alive. Teach supervisors to exercise and articulate discretion.

For lesson plans: Washington's four special circumstances are examples, not an exhaustive list, and Green's point about stolen vehicles is a permissible inference, not a rule.

Teach the posture. The court reversed summary judgment and ordered a new trial against the officers; it did not find a Fourth Amendment violation. The City's verdict stands.

applications.title: Suspicion of theft fills in the stop, not the tier
applications.body: The court held that Washington and Green clearly established that reasonable suspicion of vehicle theft alone does not justify guns, proning, and handcuffs on compliant occupants absent a case specific need. Articulate the specific facts that justify a high risk stop before choosing it.

applications.title: Your own training showed the alternative
applications.body: LAPD trains a tactical investigatory stop from cover with weapons holstered. The court cited that less intrusive option in holding a jury could find the high risk tactics unreasonable. Know the tier below the one you are about to use.

applications.title: Handcuffs need their own reason and their own end
applications.body: Handcuffing substantially aggravates a Terry stop. The family stayed cuffed about nine minutes after an officer said the car was not stolen. Once the purpose of the detention is served, restraints come off.

applications.title: "I had no choice" is a liability theory
applications.body: The sergeant's statements that a high risk stop was a given for a cold plated car let a jury infer a routine practice and reckless disregard under the Bane Act. Exercise discretion and say why.

applications.title: Teach the posture
applications.body: The Ninth Circuit reversed summary judgment and ordered a new trial against the officers. It did not find a Fourth Amendment violation, and the defense verdict for the City on failure to train was affirmed.

quiz.q: According to the Ninth Circuit in Chinaryan, what did Washington v. Lambert and Green clearly establish for summary judgment purposes?
options: That high risk stops are never permitted on a suspected stolen vehicle
That reasonable suspicion of vehicle theft alone does not justify intrusive tactics like guns, proning, and handcuffing absent some case specific need
That officers may always handcuff occupants of a cold plated vehicle for officer safety
That only the driver, not passengers, may be detained during a stolen vehicle stop
quiz.teach: The court said those cases did not set bright line rules, but they established that suspicion of theft standing alone is not enough to justify the tactics used here. It rejected the plaintiffs' broader categorical reading too.

quiz.q: What did the court decide about the claims against the individual officers?
options: It held the officers violated the Fourth Amendment and entered judgment for the plaintiffs
It affirmed qualified immunity because the law on high risk stops was unsettled
It reversed summary judgment and ordered a new trial, because a jury could find a violation on the plaintiffs' facts and the law was clearly established
It held the City's jury verdict made any error harmless
quiz.teach: The court held the officers were not entitled to qualified immunity on the plaintiffs' version of the facts, found the harmless error argument forfeited and unpersuasive, and remanded for trial. Judge Forrest dissented on harmless error.

quiz.q: Why did the court affirm the jury verdict for the City and the LAPD on the Monell claim?
options: Because the City's high risk stop policy was held constitutional

Because the plaintiffs' proposed jury instructions misstated the law by treating Washington's examples as an exhaustive list and Green's permissible inference as a categorical rule, and the general reasonableness instruction adequately covered the theory
Because municipalities cannot be liable for failure to train
Because the officers were found not to have violated the Fourth Amendment
quiz.teach: The court compared the proposed instructions to the argument rejected in Scott v. Harris: Washington applies the Fourth Amendment reasonableness test and is not a new rule with rigid preconditions. The court did not rule on the policy's constitutionality.
